t.1.44.1: Having heard Viśvāmitra's words, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, was filled with the greatest wonder and then spoke to Viśvāmitra.
t.1.44.2: O Brahman, this most wondrous and supreme account has been narrated by you: the holy descent of Gaṅgā and the filling of the ocean.
t.1.44.3: Then that whole night passed for him, together with Saumitri, as he reflected upon the auspicious tale told by Viśvāmitra.
t.1.44.4: Then, at clear daybreak, Rāghava, the subduer of foes, spoke these words to the great sage Viśvāmitra, who had completed his morning rites.
t.1.44.5: The blessed night has passed, and what was most worth hearing has been heard. That night has become like a mere moment, O great ascetic, for me as I pondered this whole tale of yours in its entirety.
t.1.44.7: Having heard those words of the great-souled Rāghava, he, together with the host of sages and with Rāghava, had a crossing arranged.
t.1.44.8: Having reached the northern bank and duly honoured the host of sages, they settled on the shore of the Gaṅgā and beheld the city of Viśālā.
t.1.44.6: Let us cross the holy river Tripathagā, the best of rivers, for this boat of the sages of meritorious deeds, comfortably spread with seats, has come swiftly, knowing that the revered one has arrived here.
t.1.44.9: Then the best of sages, together with Rāghava, quickly went to the city of Viśālā, delightful, divine and like heaven itself.
t.1.44.10: Then the very wise Rāma, with joined palms, asked the great sage Viśvāmitra about the excellent city of Viśālā.
t.1.44.11: Which royal dynasty is this in Viśālā, O great sage? I wish to hear it, blessings be upon you, for my curiosity is great indeed.
t.1.44.12: Having heard those words of Rāma, the bull among sages began to relate that ancient account of Viśāla.
t.1.44.13: Let it be heard, O Rāma, as I narrate the auspicious tale of Śakra; hear truly, O Rāghava, what took place in this very region.
t.1.44.14: Long ago, in the Kṛta age, O Rāma, there were the mighty sons of Diti, and those born of Aditi, illustrious, valiant and exceedingly righteous.
t.1.44.15: Then, O best of men, a thought arose in those great-souled ones: "How might we become immortal, free from old age, and free from disease?"
t.1.44.17: Then, having resolved upon the churning, and having made Vāsuki the rope and Mandara the churning rod, those of immeasurable might churned the ocean.
t.1.44.16: As those wise ones pondered, O Rāma, this thought came to them: "By churning the Ocean of Milk, we shall surely obtain the elixir there."
t.1.44.19: Sixty crores of those radiant Apsarases came into being, O Kākutstha, but the attendants who served them were beyond counting.
t.1.44.18: Then came the one named Dhanvantari, and the radiant Apsarases. From the churning in the waters, from that very essence, excellent women rose up, O best of men, and for that reason they became the Apsarases.
t.1.44.20: All those gods and Dānavas did not accept them, and because of that very non-acceptance they are known as belonging to all in common.
t.1.44.24: Uccaiḥśravas, the finest of horses, and the gem Kaustubha, jewel among jewels, rose up, O best of men, and likewise the supreme amṛta.
t.1.44.23: Because of that the sons of Diti became Asuras, and because of that the sons of Aditi became Suras; and the Suras were thrilled and overjoyed at receiving Vāruṇī.
t.1.44.25: Then, O Rāma, for its sake there arose a great destruction of the race, and thereupon the sons of Aditi slew the sons of Diti.
t.1.44.27: Having slain the sons of Diti and obtained the kingdom, Puraṃdara joyfully ruled the worlds, together with the hosts of ṛṣis and with the Cāraṇas.
t.1.44.26: In that terrible great war between the Daiteyas and the Ādityas, the heroic sons of Aditi fiercely slaughtered the sons of Diti.
